extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of drama/literary criticism and playwrights studying Aristotle's Poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of criteria for composing and evaluating tragic drama based on Aristotelian theory: characteristics of the tragic hero, the required emotions (pity and fear) and katharsis, requirements for subject-matter and universality, and formal rules of plot unity, magnitude, and causal sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic hero: moral resemblance and dignified elevation
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic hero must exhibit a moral resemblance to us (one of moral character), be not flawless nor meanly villainous, possess a rich and full humanity—elements others possess but blended more harmoniously or of more potent quality—and be raised above the common level in external dignity and station (a prince or famous man who falls from a height of greatness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mixture allows spectators to identify with him (make his misfortunes our own) while the hero's elevated status provides an ideal distance that removes petty material concerns and universalises the emotion. He must be human enough for sympathy but exalted enough to lift the spectator above the individual case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pity and fear (the twofold tragic emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's requirement for tragedy is the arousal of pity and fear together: 'the requirement of Aristotle is pity and fear.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both emotions are typically present in different degrees; some tragedies may predominately excite one but the full tragic effect and the katharsis depend on their union. The text discusses objections and defends that pity and fear are distinct yet allied emotions necessary for tragedy's distinctive effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of tragic fear (refracted through pity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic fear is not mere self-regarding apprehension of immediate personal danger but is refracted through pity; though it may produce a shudder or vague foreboding, it attaches to the general course of action as an image of human destiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because fear is mediated by sympathy with the hero, it becomes almost impersonal and blended with pity to inspire awe and a sense of moral inevitableness. This distinguishes Aristotelian tragic fear from a narrow personal terror.

rubrics_metrics.name: Katharsis: purgation and purification of emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy effects a katharsis — a refining or purging of pity and fear — whereby the painful, selfish, or intrusive elements of these emotions are expelled and transmuted into a pleasurable, noble emotional satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Katharsis involves both an expulsion of disturbing pain and a purifying of emotions so that they lose selfish taint; while not a direct moral education, this emotional refining may indirectly remove hindrances to virtue and enable better moral functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter must be universal/significant (capable of universalisation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic action must admit of being universalised: the incidents and fortunes represented should possess typical and universal value so pity and fear can be generalised rather than remaining petty or merely personal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private, narrowly egoistic material (e.g., exclusive love in itself) resists kathartic treatment; love can be tragic only when it connects to larger social/public issues (example: Romeo and Juliet—feud gives public stakes). The tragic subject should disclose higher laws and have consequences beyond the individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (organic unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of Action is the first requirement of tragedy: the plot must be an organic whole (ὅλον), complete (τέλειον), with parts arranged in a fixed order (τάξις) so none can be removed or transposed without disturbing the organism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity provides limit and intelligibility: the action must be a single, complete action where successive incidents are connected by an inward and causal bond (necessary or probable sequence). Unity yields both individuality and universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude (measure and proportion of length)
rubrics_metrics.description: A certain magnitude (μέγεθος) is indispensable: the work must be neither infinitely large nor infinitesimally small but of such dimensions that it can be easily taken in by the mind and retained in memory; sufficient room must exist for the natural development of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle avoids precise length rules, appealing to beauty and normal powers of memory/enjoyment. The action must evolve freely and fully so the decisive change of fortune arises through the causal sequence rather than forced compression or undue extension (e.g., Trojan War too vast even for epic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal sequence and avoidance of episodic structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Events/episodes must follow by causal (necessary or probable) sequence; succession of stirring scenes alone does not make a tragedy—avoid ἐπεισοδιώδης (episodic) plots where scenes lack inward connexion by εἰκός or necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plot's unity is tested by the inevitability of the end linked to the beginning. The drama should not present a mere series of detached scenes; each scene must contribute causally toward the catastrophe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denouement must arise from the plot itself (no mechanical devices)
rubrics_metrics.description: The λύσις (unravelling/denouement) must be brought about by the plot itself and not by mechanical devices, accident, or deus ex machina.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resorting to contrived fifth-act resolutions or external contrivances is censured; the catastrophe must seem the inevitable consequence of what has gone before—'the fifth act is an ugly evil' when used to patch up weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex vs Simple Plot (peripeteia and anagnorisis integrated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two varieties of plot: ἁπλὴ πρᾶξις (simple action) and πεπλεγμένη πρᾶξις (complex), with the latter preferred for intensifying emotions via Recognition (ἀναγνώρισις) and Reversal of Fortune (περιπέτεια), which must be woven into the plot and shown to be inevitable consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition and reversal should not be arbitrary surprises but discovered to be necessary in light of prior events; these devices should arise from the very structure (συστάσις) of the myth/plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of beginning, middle, and end (structural requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'whole' has beginning, middle, and end: the beginning does not itself follow anything by causal necessity (relative starting point), the middle follows and precedes (causally linked), and the end follows something and has nothing following it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The beginning should not force an endless retrogression of antecedents; the poet must choose a point that makes the action complete in itself. Definitions aim to exclude beginnings that demand prior causes ad infinitum, endings that fail to conclude, and middles unconnected to beginning or end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic manifestation of unity: convergence to a single end
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity is manifested in the causal connection of parts and in the direction of the whole action toward a single end; all minor effects are subordinated to an ever-growing unity so that the end reveals the meaning of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The supreme test of unity is the concentrated impression that each scene 'contributes its fraction of impulse towards the inevitable catastrophe' and that the structure is organic rather than mechanical or haphazard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate emotional distance and universalising effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy should place the hero at an ideal distance from the spectator so that immediate reality's pressure is removed, allowing emotions to be disengaged from petty self-interests and universalised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distance 'refines' tragic emotions: victims' sufferings encourage spectators to forget personal cares and to identify with humanity at large, enabling katharsis; fear and pity are thereby purged of selfish elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of narrowly self-absorbed motives (e.g., isolated love)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotions or motives that are exclusive and self-centred resist kathartic treatment; the feelings excited must be based in permanent, objective realities and not in individual caprice or sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus ordinary love stories rarely produce the highest tragedy unless embedded in larger social or public consequences that raise the case to universal significance (e.g., Romeo and Juliet's family feud gives public stakes).
